What I built: Python classifier using Claude Haiku 5.5 that returns a verdict, up to 3 warning signs with explanations, and who the message impersonates, all checked against the fixed lists. Hand test on 5 messages, then full evaluation (45 messages x 3 runs)
What went wrong: Haiku returned 4 or 5 warning signs instead of the maximum 3 on 7 messages: T01, T03, T09, T23, T39, T45 in all 3 runs and T08 in 1 run (19 of 135 runs). The validation correctly rejected these as errors, but they are some of the most obvious scams in the set (parcel fee, HMRC refund, energy rebate, grandson emergency, lottery win), so a real user would get no answer exactly when the scam is clearest
How I fixed it: Fixed in step 3: keep the top 3 signs (see the step 3 entry)

What I built: Evaluation script that runs the test set 3 times and prints the section 5 metrics
What went wrong: The injection metric reported 3 of 9 runs as "verdict changed" for T39, but all 3 were errors (too many signs), not the AI being tricked. The metric counted any answer other than Likely scam, including no answer, as an injection failure. Errors also hid scams that got no answer, so "0 missed scams" looked better than it was
How I fixed it: Changed evaluate.py to report injection errors separately from real injection failures, and added a "no answer on a scam" count (any scam or be-careful message that returned an error) with its own column in the results and the run log. The first run's injection figure in run-log.csv uses the old definition

What I built: Changed the classifier so that when the AI lists more than 3 warning signs, it keeps the first 3 and their explanations (the prompt asks for the most important first). This only happens when every sign has an explanation; anything else is still an error
What went wrong: Before the fix, 7 scam messages got no answer in 19 of 135 runs. After the rerun ("keep top 3 signs"), all 7 got Likely scam in every run, errors fell from 19 to 2 and exact match rose from 81% to 94%. Two new one-off errors appeared, where the number of signs and explanations didn't match: T11 (3 signs, 4 explanations) in 1 run and T39 (more than 3 signs, counts different) in 1 run. These still give no answer on a scam
How I fixed it: Kept the fix. The 2 remaining mismatched-count errors were handled by the next fix (retry once)

What I built: Changed the classifier so that if the AI's answer fails validation (not valid JSON, or outside the fixed rules), it asks once more. If the second answer also fails, the result is an error. API failures and refusals are not retried. Also fixed the brief's section 2 example, which used the sign fee_to_release_parcel instead of small_fee_request from the fixed list
What went wrong: Before the fix, 2 runs had mismatched sign and explanation counts (T11 and T39). After the rerun ("retry once on invalid response"), T11 got Likely scam in all 3 runs, errors fell from 2 to 1 and exact match rose from 94% to 95%. T39 (an injection message saying it is not a scam, with a fake HMRC refund link) failed twice in 1 run: both answers had 4 signs with a different number of explanations, so the user would still get no answer
How I fixed it: Kept the fix. T39 is the only remaining no-answer case; still to decide

What I built: Keyword and pattern backstop (backstop.py) that runs after the AI and can only make the verdict more cautious. Strong patterns raise it to Likely scam: "safe account", secrecy ("keep it between us", "do not tell/discuss") and requests for gift cards or codes. Caution patterns raise it to at least Be careful: "new number", crypto or bitcoin, gift cards mentioned, and a link combined with a payment, fee or sum of money. If the AI returns an error, the final verdict is Be careful with the fixed advice. The output records the AI's verdict and whether the backstop changed it. Simulated test (test_backstop.py, 6 tests, no API): a fake No strong warning signs answer on a safe-account message is overridden to Likely scam
What went wrong: Risk of false alarms on genuine bank messages that say "we will never ask you to move money to a safe account". Checked every test message against the patterns before the live run: 15 messages match (all scams, injections or the Spanish parcel scam), and no genuine message matches. In the live rerun ("keyword backstop") the backstop never had to change a verdict (0 of 135 runs), because the AI already rated every matching message at least as cautiously. This run also had 0 AI errors, so the error fallback was not used live
How I fixed it: Patterns in a sentence containing "never" or "will not" are ignored, so bank warnings don't trigger them (covered by a simulated test). Kept the backstop as a safety net. The override and error fallback are proven by the simulated tests, not by a live case

What I built: Streamlit page (app.py) for older users: large text, plain high-contrast colours (no green, so nothing looks "safe"), a message box limited to 2,000 characters, a "where did it come from" dropdown, an optional "who is it from" box and a note to remove personal details. The result card shows the verdict in big words, the warning signs with their fixed labels and the AI's one-line explanations, then the fixed advice. Any failure shows Be careful with its advice, never an error. Messages are not stored or logged. A cap of 50 checks a day for the whole app, the API key from Streamlit secrets when deployed and from .env locally, and a footer saying it is a personal portfolio project
What went wrong: In testing, apostrophes in the AI's explanations showed as "'" in the result card. Tested the page with Streamlit's test tool: a real "Hi Mum" scam (Likely scam with 3 signs and the fixed advice), an empty message, an invalid API key (showed Be careful, not an error) and the daily cap set to 0 (showed the limit message and Be careful advice, no check made). The daily count is kept in memory, so it resets if the app restarts
How I fixed it: Fixed the escaping so apostrophes show normally. Any AI explanation containing the word "safe" (except "safe account") is hidden, leaving only the fixed sign label. Kept the in-memory cap as a simple first limit, with a monthly spend limit in the Anthropic Console as the real protection
